A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attention-theory work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding results can be matched despite renumbering, restructuring, and substantial additions in v2.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical results and proofs, including its appendices, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A report original synthetic in-context regression experiments, including output and gradient discrepancies, prediction risks, and training trajectories in Figures 1–8.

M1.justification: The core theoretical attention operator and loss remain unchanged. v2 adds an experimental model variant with an explicit output matrix O and jointly trained O,V,K,Q parameters (Section 6 and Appendix A.1), extending the architectures documented in v1.

E1.justification: v1 studies regression distributions theoretically but performs no empirical evaluation. v2 evaluates synthetic noisy in-context linear regression with both isotropic Gaussian covariates and anisotropic covariates having covariance entries 0.5^|i-j|.

E2.justification: v2 establishes empirical comparisons absent from v1: normalized linear attention is compared with softmax attention, and Figures 2 and 6 additionally evaluate the L-Bayes-optimal estimator, described as appropriately tuned ridge regression.

E3.justification: The new experiments introduce concrete training and evaluation protocols: dimension 5, SGD with learning rate 0.001, 500,000 steps, batches of 128 prompts, and prompt-length sweeps. Measurements include output/gradient discrepancies, prediction risk at matched training and evaluation lengths, and distances between training trajectories.

E4.justification: v2 adds prompt-length sensitivity analyses of attention outputs, gradients, and parameter trajectories. Appendix A adds training-risk curves and isotropic-versus-anisotropic comparisons that examine convergence speed and irregular dynamics. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports shared random seeds for initialization and training batches, and discloses rerunning linear models with different seeds after initialization-dependent failures. It provides no repeated-run aggregates, failure counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 1–8 add measured outcomes absent from v1: output and gradient discrepancies generally decrease with prompt length; linear attention achieves lower reported risk than softmax, with narrowing gaps; and anisotropic training trajectories are less regular. Appendix A also reports occasional linear-model optimization failures.

T1.justification: v2 replaces v1's Gaussian/spherical moment arguments with general sub-Gaussian Lemma D.1, removing Proposition 3.1's additional output-moment hypothesis. It also localizes Assumption 4.2 to the relevant parameter ball, addresses singular Gaussian measures in Appendix B.1, and adds the pseudoinverse-based regression convergence extension in Appendix F.3.

C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contribution themes are retained. The contribution list and conclusion now explicitly qualify the transfer between softmax and linear attention as applying to centered Gaussian inputs, refining the earlier Gaussian-input wording.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of why explicit convergence rates require further problem-specific assumptions, interprets structured initialization as mainly technical, and discusses extension to singular covariances. Appendix A interprets anisotropy as making optimization harder and potentially requiring longer prompts, substantially expanding the applicability and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents data generation, training hyperparameters, PyTorch initialization, comparator normalization, and implementation provenance. It reports a public code repository, laptop execution, and approximately 30 minutes per architecture/prompt-length run; v1 contains no corresponding experimental reproducibility information.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the measure-based research context and explicitly credits Vuckovic et al. and Sander et al. It adds a detailed comparison with concurrent Bohbot et al., distinguishing their sharper output-moment concentration from this work's output/gradient L2 concentration and training analysis, alongside additional relevant citations.

P1.justification: Most retained exposition and proof organization remain recognizable. v2 revises section titles, related-work and conclusion paragraphs, clarifies assumptions and notation, and gives the existing initialization its own assumption label. New experiments and extensions receive dedicated sections and appendix navigation.

P2.justification: v2 introduces eight figures where v1 had no experimental plots, covering discrepancies, risks, and training trajectories. It also substantially redesigns presentation through a two-column main text, running headers, a revised title block, and an appendix contents list.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens a central concentration result by proving the moment bound assumed in v1 and adds a singular-covariance extension. Controlled finite-prompt experiments test the theoretical predictions, supported by implementation details and clearer research attribution. Missing uncertainty estimates and reruns after linear-model failures limit the empirical rankings, but the broader theoretical support and direct numerical checks constitute a substantial overall improvement.
